facts.title: A mistress and a living emblem
facts.body: Leonardo painted Cecilia Gallerani, mistress of Ludovico Sforza, around 1489–91. The ermine in her arms is both pet and heraldic pun on purity and on Ludovico’s Order of the Ermine.

facts.title: Cecilia Gallerani
facts.body: Young, alert, and turning — Cecilia is caught mid-attention. Leonardo invents a living portrait, not a static court mask.

facts.title: The ermine as double meaning
facts.body: The animal’s white coat signaled purity; its presence also nods to Ludovico il Moro’s chivalric order. Form and politics share one fur.

facts.title: A glance offstage
facts.body: Cecilia looks toward something we cannot see — a conversation entering the frame from outside.

facts.title: A precise hand
facts.body: Her right hand rests on the ermine with anatomical care. Leonardo’s study of tendons shows even in a court portrait.

facts.title: Black beads against skin
facts.body: A simple black necklace draws a dark line across the throat, sharpening the face against the void behind her.

facts.title: Blue sleeve, gold trim
facts.body: The sleeve’s volume and trim advertise Milanese fashion while giving Leonardo folds to model in light.

facts.title: A ground like night
facts.body: The dark background isolates figure and animal — a theatrical void rather than a room.
